BOW.Quote: At 25 Vermont nests observed by videography, one female fed at each nest, with two provisioning males most common (60%), followed by nests with one provisioning male (20%), nests with three males (16%), and nests with four males (4%; VCE). Four males documented to feed at >1 nest within single breeding season, and three males fed two broods simultaneously (nests 186–443 m apart). One male simultaneously provisioned at two nests 443 m apart, shared feeding of nestlings at first nest, was sole male feeder at second nest. First nest fledged 3 d after second nest hatched; male then left care of fledglings to the other male and fed second brood at nearly twice the rate as he had fed young at first nest. Individual female, total male, and total adult provisioning rates did not differ between nests with single and multiple male feeders. The number of male feeders was negatively correlated to prey abundance on female home ranges, suggesting that females might balance the cost of low prey abundance by copulating with multiple males and attracting male feeders (Strong et al. 2004). Overall, females fed nestlings at more than twice the rate of males (Goetz et al 2003). Male feeding rates increased with nestling age until day 7–8 and then decreased until fledging. Some males did not feed at nests in which they sired young, and some males fed at nests in which they sired no young (Goetz et al. 2003). Multiple male feeders also reported at nests in Quebec (Y. Aubry) and New Brunswick (Askanas 2012). In highlands of New Brunswick, 78% of nests had two or more male feeders (Askanas 2012). At five nests females provided 57±15% of the feeds at a nest, individual males 21±9%. In Quebec three males attended two different nests in one breeding season (Y. Aubry unpubl.). I

BOW.Quote: Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). BOW.Quote: Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).
